query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: In multi‐element near‐equiatomic nanoparticles, the preservation of structural and chemical stability at high service temperatures is governed by the balance between high configurational entropy, which stabilizes the random solid‐solution phase, and the enhanced surface diffusion associated with high surface-to-volume ratios that promotes elemental segregation. Thus, if surface diffusion is mitigated (for example, via a passivating surface treatment that reduces effective diffusion), the nanoparticles will retain their homogeneous composition and crystal structure under operation.
generation.material_initial_state: Near-equiatomic, high-entropy (random solid-solution) nanoparticles with high surface-to-volume ratios.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin, inert surface passivation layer (or otherwise reduce effective surface area, such as by slightly increasing particle size) to impede surface diffusion and segregation.
generation.conditions: Service temperatures ranging from 773–1173 K for catalytic applications and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric applications; experiments conducted under inert or controlled atmospheres to reduce extraneous chemical effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoparticle’s high surface-to-volume ratio mediates the competition between configurational entropy (favoring homogeneity) and surface diffusion (promoting elemental segregation).
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, high configurational entropy favors the retention of a random solid-solution structure; however, the increased mobility of surface atoms in small nanoparticles amplifies the likelihood of atomic reordering and elemental segregation. A passivating surface layer reduces surface mobility, thereby sustaining the homogeneous distribution imposed by entropy, and mitigating the onset of phase separation or the formation of segregated chemical domains.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with the surface passivation intervention will exhibit reduced elemental segregation (as evidenced by spatially resolved compositional analysis) and maintain their phase integrity, leading to stable catalytic or thermoelectric performance relative to uncoated nanoparticles which will show signs of phase decomposition or segregation after identical heat treatments.
generation.baseline: Uncoated nanoparticles with the same near-equiatomic composition, which are expected to show more pronounced surface-driven segregation and structural degradation under the same thermal conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for nanoparticles with near-equiatomic, high-entropy compositions and within the specified temperature ranges; deviations may occur in systems with very different surface chemistries, particle sizes, or where additional thermochemical effects are present.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent to which surface passivation reduces diffusion and prevents segregation is not precisely known; additional variables such as the exact nature of the passivating layer and the detailed interatomic interactions in multi-element systems introduce uncertainty in the magnitude of the effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of near-equiatomic high-entropy nanoparticles with identical initial compositions and size distributions. One set receives a thin, inert passivating surface layer while the other remains uncoated. Subject both sets to thermal treatment at target service temperatures (e.g., 900 K for catalytic, 1500 K for thermoelectric conditions) for an extended period, under controlled atmosphere conditions.
measurements: Spatially resolved elemental mapping (e.g., by TEM-EDS or atom probe tomography) before and after thermal treatment.
Phase identification via X-ray diffraction to assess any structural transitions or formation of secondary phases.
Catalytic or thermoelectric performance metrics to detect any degradation correlated with compositional changes.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the passivated nanoparticles do not show significant improvement in preservation of the homogeneous phase or performance compared to the uncoated nanoparticles (i.e., if both sets exhibit similar levels of elemental segregation or structural degradation after thermal treatment), then the hypothesis that controlling surface diffusion via passivation is key to preserving stability under service conditions will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs), complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), and multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) are the most common names of a new group of materials [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ] introduced by Yeh et al. [ [6] ] and Cantor et al. [ [7] ] in the beginning of this century. Many definitions were proposed for such materials, but in general they consist of multiple (usually at least five) elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic composition [ [2] ]. This approach is different from the traditional alloy design using one (or maximum two) principal element and other minor elements. The presence of many elements in equiatomic (or near) composition leads to high mixing entropy and thus to many interesting properties [ [2] , [5] ]. One of such effects is the existence of a random solid solution and simple body centered cubic (bcc) or faced centered cubic (fcc) structure. Recently HEAs with hexagonal closed packed (hcp) structure have been reported as well [ [8] , [9] ]. A new approach to HEA design using the valence electron concentration (VEC) was recently proposed with the aim of increasing the plasticity of these alloys [ [10] , [11] ]. Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.
